title: Northstar Support x Redwood — Dedicated tiering + throughput SLO demo
next_steps: Redwood to send a one-pager with customer-facing throughput SLO language (including measurement window + exclusions) and the credit remedy summary.
Northstar to share target model(s), context length distribution, and peak concurrency so Redwood can propose a Standard vs Plus sizing recommendation.
Redwood to provision a short Dedicated trial in us-west and run a benchmark with Northstar prompts (streaming + non-streaming).
Schedule security/SLA review with Northstar procurement once tier selection is narrowed (Standard vs Plus).
action_items: Markus Klein: Send links/screenshots to the Dedicated monitoring dashboard panels shown (throughput floor, saturation, queue depth) by EOD 2025-02-06.
Lauren Bishop: Share draft Dedicated tier definitions (Standard/Plus/Premium) and what is “in writing” vs “best effort” by 2025-02-07.
Stephanie Nguyen: Follow up with pricing bands for the candidate shape(s) in us-west and lead times by 2025-02-07.
Daniel Cho: Provide Northstar’s current token accounting approach and how they report success internally (req/s vs tok/s) by 2025-02-10.
body:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Northstar Support x Redwood — Dedicated tiering + throughput SLO demo
Date: 2025-02-05
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 49 min

Attendees
- Stephanie Nguyen (Redwood) — Sales
- Markus Klein (Redwood) — Solutions / SE
- Lauren Bishop (Redwood) — Product (Dedicated)
- Priya Shah (Northstar Support) — VP Eng
- Daniel Cho (Northstar Support) — Platform Eng Mgr
- Maya Rodriguez (Northstar Support) — ML Lead
- Evan Brooks (Northstar Support) — Procurement

---
Auto-summary (generated)
Northstar asked how Redwood’s Dedicated throughput commitments are measured and what happens if Redwood misses. Redwood demoed Dedicated monitoring: committed throughput floor tracking, saturation signals, and per-deployment token accounting (streaming vs non-streaming). Discussion covered tiers (Standard/Plus/Premium), burst behavior, exclusions (customer throttling, unsupported model/version changes, cold start), and credit remedies. Next steps include sharing customer-facing SLO language, a tier recommendation based on Northstar’s workload, and a short trial/benchmark.

Topics
- Dedicated tiers overview (Standard / Plus / Premium)
- Throughput metric: tokens/sec vs requests/sec, and how streaming is counted
- Measurement window and what counts as an SLO “miss”
- Exclusions: customer-side throttles, invalid requests, model changes, warmup
- Credits / remedies and escalation path
- Dashboard walkthrough: throughput floor, saturation, queue depth, admission control

Questions captured
- “Is the guarantee tokens per second or requests per second?”
- “How do you count streaming? Is that output tokens only? Do prompt tokens count?”
- “If we burst above committed throughput, do you throttle or bill? Both?”
- “If you miss the floor for 20 minutes, do we get credits automatically?”
- “What if we run two models in the same Dedicated deployment?”

---
Transcript

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. Alright, I’m gonna get us started. Thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is pretty simple: walk you through how Dedicated looks in the console, how we’re thinking about tiers, and then the big one, how throughput is measured and what we do if we miss it.

[00:18] Priya Shah: Yep. That’s exactly what we need. We’re getting pressure internally to have something in writing that’s not just “best effort.”

[00:27] Stephanie Nguyen: Makes sense.

[00:29] Markus Klein: And I’ll drive the screen share in a sec. Just a quick check, can everyone see my screen when I share?

[00:35] Daniel Cho: Not yet.

[00:37] Markus Klein: Sharing now.

[00:41] Markus Klein: Okay, this is our Console. I’m in a demo tenant, but it’s the same layout customers get. On the left you’ll see Deployments, then Dedicated, and we have a specific view per deployment. This one is “northstar-dedicated-usw2” — obviously fake name.

[00:59] Maya Rodriguez: This is the thing we wouldn’t have on hosted, right?

[01:02] Markus Klein: You get some of it on hosted, but Dedicated adds a few panels: committed throughput floor, pool saturation, queue depth, and the tier entitlements.

[01:11] Stephanie Nguyen: And just to anchor: tiers are Standard, Plus, Premium. Standard is basically committed throughput with regional placement, Plus adds explicit burst policy and tighter support targets, Premium adds higher headroom posture and more failover options. Lauren can add color there.

[01:27] Lauren Bishop: Yeah. The short version is: as you go up tiers, you’re buying more predictability. Not just higher tokens/sec, but the operational posture behind it.

[01:38] Evan Brooks: When you say “predictability,” is that like credits if you miss? Or just someone picks up the phone.

[01:44] Lauren Bishop: Both. There’s the measurement and there’s the remedy.

[01:49] Priya Shah: Great. Let’s dig into measurement then.

[01:53] Markus Klein: Yep. So, panel one: “Throughput (deployment)”. We track tokens per second at the deployment boundary. That’s output tokens per second primarily, and we can show input tokens too, but the SLO is anchored on output tok/s.

[02:09] Daniel Cho: Wait— output only? We care about total tokens. Like we get billed on both, no?

[02:14] Markus Klein: Billing is total, yes. But for the guarantee we found output is the most stable and maps better to user perceived speed. That said, we can also define it as “generated tokens” explicitly so there’s no confusion.

[02:28] Maya Rodriguez: How do you handle streaming? Because streaming makes it feel fast even if total completion time is long.

[02:35] Markus Klein: Totally. In streaming, we count tokens as they are emitted. There was a… I’ll just say we’ve done some work to make sure we don’t double-count. But in this view, you can see “streamed_output_tokens/sec” and “non_streamed_output_tokens/sec” broken out.

[02:52] Priya Shah: That implies you’re not looking at “request completed per second”. It’s really tok/s.

[02:58] Markus Klein: Correct. For chat and generation routes we use tok/s. For embeddings it’s slightly different; it’s like vectors/sec or input tokens/sec, but for this Dedicated discussion we’re talking primarily generation.

[03:12] Lauren Bishop: There’s also an ADR internally on why tok/s is canonical. I can share a simplified version.

[03:19] Evan Brooks: We don’t need the internal doc, we need the contract language.

[03:23] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep, fair.

[03:25] Markus Klein: So, here’s the “Committed throughput floor” widget. In this demo it’s set at 1,200 tok/s over a 30-minute rolling window.

[03:35] Daniel Cho: Rolling 30 minutes. Okay. Is that like p50, p95, what is it?

[03:41] Markus Klein: It’s time-averaged throughput. Think: total output tokens over the window divided by window seconds, and we compare it to the committed floor. It’s not a latency percentile guarantee.

[03:54] Priya Shah: So if we are idle for part of that window, we’re below the floor. That would be weird.

[03:59] Markus Klein: Great callout. We only evaluate during “eligible time,” meaning when you are sending requests and we are not throttling you for customer-configured limits. Basically, you need to be demanding at least the floor. If you’re not asking for it, we don’t say you’re “under.”

[04:18] Daniel Cho: So it’s like: if we request less than the floor, you ignore it. If we request more than the floor, you try to meet it.

[04:24] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[04:26] Maya Rodriguez: How do you determine “requested throughput” on streaming though? Like you can always open more connections.

[04:33] Markus Klein: We treat that as concurrency + backlog. You’ll see this “queue depth” panel. If queue depth is near zero, you’re not backlogged. If it’s consistently positive and we’re below committed tok/s, that’s a red flag.

[04:48] Priya Shah: That makes sense.

[04:50] Evan Brooks: Let me ask the finance question. If you miss it for, say, an hour, what happens? Is it a credit? Is it automatic?

[04:59] Lauren Bishop: The current proposal is service credits tied to SLO compliance, with a threshold so we’re not crediting for a two-minute blip. Likely evaluated monthly, but we also have an incident workflow when it’s sustained.

[05:15] Evan Brooks: Monthly credits are fine as long as it’s measurable and not arguable.

[05:20] Stephanie Nguyen: Agree. We’re trying hard to make it not a “he said she said.”

[05:24] Daniel Cho: What are the exclusions? Like, I’m guessing “bad prompts” doesn’t count, right?

[05:30] Markus Klein: Exclusions are things like: invalid requests, unsupported model changes, customer-side throttles, and cold start / warmup periods when you just provision a deployment.

[05:41] Maya Rodriguez: Wait, “unsupported model changes” — can we swap models on the same deployment?

[05:46] Lauren Bishop: On Dedicated you can run multiple models, but the SLO is defined per deployment and is tied to a pinned model/version set. If you change that materially, we need to rebaseline. Otherwise customers can game it by switching to a heavier model and saying we’re violating.

[06:05] Priya Shah: That’s fair. We would likely pin anyway. We’re debating Llama 70B vs something smaller.

[06:12] Markus Klein: Right. And the shape choice matters.

[06:15] Stephanie Nguyen: Before we go too deep on shapes, can I confirm your main user flow? Is it agentic chat for support tickets, or summarization, or both?

[06:24] Priya Shah: Both. Summarization on every ticket, and then agent assist for about 20% of tickets.

[06:32] Daniel Cho: Peak is Monday mornings. It’s spiky.

[06:36] Markus Klein: That’s where “burst” comes in.

[06:39] Evan Brooks: Yeah, burst. This is the other thing I need to understand. Are you letting them burst “for free” or are you charging?

[06:46] Stephanie Nguyen: So, burst is tier-dependent. In Standard, burst exists but it’s best effort—meaning if there is slack capacity in the pool, you can exceed your committed floor, but we don’t promise a specific burst factor.

[06:59] Lauren Bishop: Plus introduces an explicit burst policy. Example: up to 1.5x committed for up to N minutes in an hour, subject to a max concurrency. Premium can do higher, with more reserved headroom.

[07:12] Evan Brooks: And billing for burst?

[07:15] Lauren Bishop: Typically Dedicated is a monthly commit for the reserved capacity. If you consume burst from a shared burst pool, there can be metering for burst usage depending on your contract. We’re finalizing that.

[07:30] Daniel Cho: So you might both throttle and bill?

[07:33] Markus Klein: More like: we don’t throttle within committed. Beyond committed, we attempt to serve via burst. If burst pool is saturated, then yes, admission control can kick in to protect other customers and your own SLO floor.

[07:47] Maya Rodriguez: What does admission control look like? Like 429s?

[07:50] Markus Klein: It can be 429, or it can be queueing with a cap and then shedding. We prefer to surface a clear “over capacity” signal.

[08:00] Priya Shah: That’s okay, but we need to know: does the guarantee include latency? We’re currently targeting first token under 500ms.

[08:08] Markus Klein: This specific SLO is throughput, not latency. We can discuss latency targets separately, but it’s harder to guarantee across your prompt distribution.

[08:18] Priya Shah: Understood.

[08:20] Markus Klein: Let me show you the SLO status panel. It says “Compliant: 99.5% of eligible minutes, last 7 days.” If it dips, it links to incident timeline and the root cause notes.

[08:33] Daniel Cho: Eligible minutes again means: we’re demanding and you’re not blocked by our own limits.

[08:38] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[08:40] Evan Brooks: How do you prove to us you’re measuring correctly? I’m thinking audits.

[08:46] Lauren Bishop: We expose the metrics in the console and export them via the API. We also can provide monthly reporting. For regulated customers, we can map this into audit logs.

[08:58] Priya Shah: Not regulated, but we do want transparency.

[09:03] Markus Klein: Also we tag metrics by deployment_id, model, and region. So you can match it against your request logs.

[09:12] Maya Rodriguez: Can I ask about prompt caching / prefix caching? Does that affect tok/s measurement? Because caching could make you look better.

[09:20] Markus Klein: Great question. Throughput is observed at the output. If caching reduces compute, it can increase output tok/s, yes. But that’s actually beneficial to you. We don’t “cheat” the metric, it’s still tokens delivered.

[09:34] Daniel Cho: But if you batch requests, you might increase throughput while increasing tail latency.

[09:39] Markus Klein: Correct tradeoff. Dedicated lets us tune batching. In Plus/Premium we generally keep tighter latency caps and rely on headroom rather than aggressive batching.

[09:52] Priya Shah: That’s part of why we’re considering Dedicated at all.

[09:56] Stephanie Nguyen: Exactly.

[10:00] Markus Klein: Okay, let’s talk tier options at a high level. Standard: committed throughput floor, single region, standard support. Plus: committed floor + burst entitlement + more proactive monitoring. Premium: highest commitment, stronger failover posture, and fastest response.

[10:17] Evan Brooks: “Failover posture” is vague. Do you mean multi-region active-active?

[10:22] Lauren Bishop: For Premium we can do options like warm standby in a second region, or reserved spare nodes within region. Active-active is possible but depends on region supply and your architecture.

[10:34] Priya Shah: We’d probably be fine with in-region HA plus a plan for regional incident. Not necessarily active-active day one.

[10:43] Markus Klein: That maps well to Plus or Premium depending on the numbers.

[10:48] Daniel Cho: Can we go back to the credit question? If you miss, do we open a ticket or is it automatic.

[10:55] Lauren Bishop: It’s not fully automated today. Operationally, we’d detect via burn-rate alerts and open an incident. Credits are handled through Support/CS with a clear policy. The goal is to make it straightforward, not negotiation.

[11:13] Evan Brooks: I’d strongly prefer automatic.

[11:16] Stephanie Nguyen: Noted. A lot of customers ask that. We’re moving in that direction, but we want to avoid false positives first.

[11:25] Maya Rodriguez: What’s a false positive in this context?

[11:28] Markus Klein: Streaming accounting issues, customer retry storms, or cases where a client timeout makes it look like we’re underdelivering when actually the network path dropped. Also if you’re throttling yourself with an API gateway.

[11:43] Daniel Cho: That’s actually real for us. We have Envoy limits.

[11:46] Markus Klein: Exactly. That’s why exclusions include customer-side throttling and client-side cancellation.

[11:54] Priya Shah: We should define “client cancellation” carefully. Sometimes we cancel because it’s too slow.

[12:01] Lauren Bishop: Agreed. The language usually says: cancellations before first token are excluded if initiated by the client, but we can carve out cases where we exceeded agreed timeouts. This is where the contract detail matters.

[12:17] Evan Brooks: That’s the part legal will push on.

[12:20] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood.

[12:22] Markus Klein: Let me show the incident drilldown. Here’s a sample incident: “GPU pool saturation - usw2”. You can see the graph: demand above capacity, admission control engaged, throughput floor started to dip, and then mitigation was adding capacity.

[12:40] Daniel Cho: That’s helpful. Is that the same pool we’d be on?

[12:44] Markus Klein: In Dedicated, you’re on a dedicated pool. But depending on tier, burst may come from a shared burst pool.

[12:52] Maya Rodriguez: Shared burst pool makes me nervous.

[12:55] Lauren Bishop: It’s optional and it’s capacity-accounted. Premium customers may have a dedicated burst buffer, effectively.

[13:06] Priya Shah: Okay.

[13:08] Stephanie Nguyen: Can we talk numbers briefly? What floor do you think you need?

[13:13] Daniel Cho: We did a rough estimate. Peak is like 300 concurrent chats, but they’re not all generating huge outputs. Most are 150-300 tokens.

[13:25] Maya Rodriguez: And summaries are like 200 tokens output, input around 2k tokens sometimes.

[13:32] Markus Klein: Input size affects compute, but the SLO is output tok/s. Still, to size the shape we need both.

[13:41] Priya Shah: Right.

[13:42] Markus Klein: Typically for Llama 70B class models, you’ll see fewer tok/s per GPU than smaller models. For support workloads, many customers use a 7B-14B for summaries, then a bigger model selectively.

[13:57] Maya Rodriguez: We’ve considered that.

[14:00] Evan Brooks: If we do two models, do we have two SLOs?

[14:04] Lauren Bishop: If they’re on the same deployment and share the same pool, the SLO is at the deployment level. If you want per-model guarantees, we’d separate deployments or define per-route commitments.

[14:17] Daniel Cho: That’s important.

[14:19] Markus Klein: We can also tag throughput by route in the dashboard so you can see where tokens are going.

[14:27] Priya Shah: Okay.

[14:29] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s pause and see if there are any hard requirements around being able to say “we guarantee X.” Is that a procurement need or an internal SRE requirement.

[14:40] Evan Brooks: Procurement. We need contract language.

[14:43] Priya Shah: And internal. If this powers customer-facing chat, we can’t have it degrade unpredictably.

[14:51] Markus Klein: That’s where Dedicated is a good fit.

[14:54] Maya Rodriguez: Can you explain the measurement window again. You said 30 minutes rolling. Is that fixed across tiers?

[15:02] Lauren Bishop: Likely the same window across tiers, but Premium may have stricter alerting and response times. We’re trying to keep measurement consistent to avoid confusion.

[15:14] Daniel Cho: Do you do like 5 minutes? Because 30 minutes is kind of long if we’re down.

[15:19] Markus Klein: Alerting is faster than the credit window. Internally we can alert on 5-minute burn rate and page. The SLO evaluation can still be 30-minute for stability.

[15:33] Priya Shah: That’s good.

[15:35] Evan Brooks: If you miss for 20 minutes during peak, we care a lot, even if you’re fine the rest of the month.

[15:43] Lauren Bishop: Totally. That would be an incident.

[15:46] Markus Klein: You would see it here, and Support would proactively reach out on Plus/Premium.

[15:53] Stephanie Nguyen: And to be transparent, Standard is more reactive. Plus is where proactive comms and defined burst tends to show up.

[16:05] Priya Shah: So Plus seems like the likely tier.

[16:08] Daniel Cho: Probably.

[16:10] Maya Rodriguez: I still want clarity on what tokens count. Prompt tokens not included in the guarantee, but billing includes them. If we do long contexts, could we still be “compliant” but slow?

[16:22] Markus Klein: Potentially yes. That’s why we’ll do sizing guidance with your context distribution, and we can set soft limits on max context for the deployment.

[16:34] Priya Shah: Okay, so we can constrain max context to keep predictability.

[16:38] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[16:40] Evan Brooks: And if we exceed that max context?

[16:43] Markus Klein: We reject or route to a different deployment. Depends on configuration.

[16:50] Daniel Cho: If you reject, does that count against SLO?

[16:53] Lauren Bishop: If the request is out of policy (too large, unsupported), it’s excluded.

[17:00] Priya Shah: That’s reasonable.

[17:03] Markus Klein: Another panel: “Saturation signals.” GPU utilization, KV cache pressure, and queue time. This helps you tell if you’re hitting the floor because of your workload or because we’re constrained.

[17:18] Maya Rodriguez: KV cache pressure… does that show if we do multi-turn chat and keep long histories?

[17:23] Markus Klein: Yes, it reflects that. It’s not perfect, but it correlates with long contexts and many concurrent sessions.

[17:33] Daniel Cho: Is KV cache pressure the thing that makes throughput drop off a cliff?

[17:37] Markus Klein: It can. Especially if we start evicting.

[17:41] Priya Shah: So we’ll need guidance.

[17:44] Stephanie Nguyen: Which is what Markus and the Solutions team do in onboarding.

[17:49] Evan Brooks: Okay. Let’s circle back: credits. What’s the magnitude? Like 5%? 10%?

[17:56] Lauren Bishop: The typical structure is a percentage of monthly fees, scaled by severity. For example: if compliance falls below threshold, credits in bands. I don’t want to quote numbers without legal review.

[18:10] Evan Brooks: Understood, but you can send a draft policy.

[18:13] Lauren Bishop: Yep.

[18:15] Markus Klein: Also, we’ll specify escalation. If the throughput floor is below commitment and queue depth is positive for X minutes, we page SRE and Infra.

[18:27] Daniel Cho: Do we get access to those runbooks? Like can we see what you’re doing.

[18:32] Markus Klein: Not the internal runbooks, but we can share a customer-facing incident response process and status page updates.

[18:40] Priya Shah: Okay.

[18:42] Maya Rodriguez: One more streaming question. You said you count tokens as emitted. If we use tool calls / function calling, does that change the token accounting?

[18:52] Markus Klein: Not materially. It’s still tokens. Structured output may have slightly different behavior, but it’s accounted the same.

[19:01] Daniel Cho: And if you do speculative decoding or whatever, is that included.

[19:05] Markus Klein: Only delivered tokens count. Not internal speculation.

[19:10] Priya Shah: Great.

[19:12] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ve talked a lot about the SLO. Should we cover briefly how this compares to Bedrock or Azure in terms of what they put in writing?

[19:21] Evan Brooks: Sure.

[19:23] Stephanie Nguyen: In our experience, the hyperscalers usually give you an uptime SLA, sometimes latency, but throughput is squishier unless you do dedicated capacity with a lot of caveats. Our goal is to make it explicit and measurable, with a tiered offering.

[19:39] Priya Shah: That’s consistent with our experience.

[19:42] Maya Rodriguez: We also looked at Replicate, but it’s not… like the predictability wasn’t there.

[19:47] Markus Klein: Yeah, different product.

[19:49] Daniel Cho: Together had some dedicated options, but again, not sure about metrics.

[19:54] Stephanie Nguyen: Right.

[19:56] Markus Klein: Okay, last thing from me: exports. We can export “committed vs delivered throughput” and “burst usage.” That’s useful for your own reporting and if finance wants to see if you’re paying for headroom you don’t need.

[20:12] Evan Brooks: Yes. That’s huge.

[20:14] Priya Shah: Can we get that via API?

[20:17] Markus Klein: Yes.

[20:18] Daniel Cho: Is it real-time or delayed?

[20:20] Markus Klein: Metrics are near real-time (couple minutes). Billing exports are daily.

[20:28] Maya Rodriguez: If we do the trial, can we test both Standard and Plus.

[20:33] Stephanie Nguyen: We can structure it as a Plus-like posture for the POC so you experience burst and monitoring, then pricing can reflect the tier.

[20:43] Evan Brooks: Okay.

[20:44] Priya Shah: Timeline: we’d like to choose in March.

[20:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[20:49] Markus Klein: I’ll stop sharing in a second. Any other questions before recap?

[20:54] Daniel Cho: One: what if you’re below throughput because our request mix changed. Like we suddenly have longer outputs.

[21:02] Lauren Bishop: If you change the workload materially, the observed tokens/sec could change. The commitment is about delivered tokens/sec, so if you demand it, we still need to meet it. But if you start running a much heavier model or exceed context constraints, that’s where rebaseline comes in.

[21:22] Daniel Cho: Okay.

[21:23] Maya Rodriguez: So commitments are tied to pinned model and within context guidelines.

[21:28] Lauren Bishop: Exactly.

[21:30] Evan Brooks: And if you run out of GPU supply in that region.

[21:34] Stephanie Nguyen: Then we’d talk lead times. For Premium we reserve more. For Standard/Plus we can still do it, but certain shapes in certain regions can have lead time. We’ll be transparent.

[21:47] Priya Shah: Okay.

[21:49] Stephanie Nguyen: Recap on next steps: Markus will send the dashboard panels and what you saw today. Lauren will send the tier definitions and draft SLO language including measurement and exclusions and how credits work. I’ll send pricing ranges for Plus in us-west and what lead times look like. And Daniel, if you can send us your prompt/context distribution, we’ll propose a sizing.

[22:12] Daniel Cho: Yep.

[22:13] Maya Rodriguez: I’ll send some examples too.

[22:16] Evan Brooks: And please include the credit language. That’s what I need to show legal.

[22:20] Lauren Bishop: Will do.

[22:22] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Thanks everyone.

[22:25] Markus Klein: Thanks.

[22:26] Priya Shah: Thank you.

---
Note: Call ended early in transcript export; remaining time included off-record scheduling and calendaring per participants.
